description: Solving problems within our community, one line of code at a time.
summary: We developed an offline optimization engine for the agricultural field allotment process that allows farmers to precisely organize their land usage according to the soil conditions. This spatial zoning system was developed in response to the decreasing level of farmland across the US. With smaller fields to work with than ever, our tool allows farmers to effectively organize land usage in a way that produces the best results based on soil information.
details:
Our project uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript for frontend development; Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui for styling; MapLibre GL JS and deck.gl for interactive geospatial visualization; Python and FastAPI for backend development; Pandas, NumPy, and Xarray for data processing; Pyomo and HiGHS for mathematical optimization; XGBoost and scikit-learn for machine learning and predictive modeling; and GeoPandas, Rasterio, and Shapely for geospatial data processing. Additionally, we used PostgreSQL and PostGIS for database infrastructure, and Python-based processing and deployment (originally, we used a Streamlit dashboard, but we realized that there was a much lower technical barrier if we built the frontend from Scratch; it would also allow us to customize the interface a bit more to make it more user friendly).

We learned a ton from the implementation of features that were designed for farmers, and put a lot of effort into agriculture-oriented design. We wanted to ensure that our project was not only technically advanced, but also extremely intuitive and to understand. We thought from the perspective of our target audience: farmers. The app is designed to be practical for farmers who may not have that much experience with technology usage. We thought of different variables like water availability, soil health, crop compatibility, climate risks, and economic sustainability when building the optimization models and recommendation system.

Our project uses NASA Earth observation data to analyze environmental conditions and help farmers determine which crop rotations would be most suitable for their fields. Farmers can select their location, enter information about their current crops and available resources, and receive recommendations based on their individual needs and priorities. We also added interactive visualizations and climate simulations that allow users to compare different crop rotations and understand how changes in temperature, rainfall, and irrigation availability could affect their agricultural outcomes. We could have just settled at a simple crop rotation system, but we went further than that; farmers can draw out their field locations and view an in depth analysis.

One of the most creative parts of our project is combining multiple scientific models and optimization algorithms with an interactive agricultural twin. Instead of just giving a list of recommended crops, we desired for farmers to look at different scenarios and understand why certain rotations were recommended. This way, they could make their own informed decisions through the proposed strategies on the dashboard.

Our objective with NASA OASIS is to make advanced agricultural and crop rotation technology more accessible to farmers, not just in the United States, but globally. We hope to help farmers conserve water, improve soil health, reduce climate-related risks, and maintain agricultural productivity with decreasing farmland availability. We believe that our project demonstrates how publicly available space-based data can be used to address real-world agricultural challenges and support more sustainable farming practices.
